newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coffee price may reduce need for ACPC export cuts.
newsitem.headline: Coffee price may reduce need for ACPC export cuts.

text.p: Rising coffee prices could mean members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) will find little reason to cut exports substantially when they meet on January 23, traders and delegates attending an international coffee seminar in Rio de Janeiro said.

The ACPC session also to be held in Rio de Janeiro was called at the request of African producers who in December said they wanted a cut of around 2.5 million 60-kg bags in ACPC member exports between January and June this year.
Traders have anticipated any reductions would be largely centred on robusta coffee, especially given a recent rise in arabica prices.

But with the London robusta coffee market today rising to prices not seen since September, some producer delegates attending the seminar feel there may now be less of a need to tighten supply of robustas to the market.
ACPC president Rubens Barbosa has declined comment on the likely outcome of the ACPC session on Thursday.
However, in an interview with reporters, he noted the evident tightening of supply in the arabica market as seen by the recent upward move in prices.
"Prices are now rising and begining to reflect the tight situation in the market, particularly in arabica coffee. In robusta there is a very little excess supply," Barbosa said.

One of the key factors in Thursday's discussions will be the stance of Indonesia, the world's largest robusta producer, currently with an export quota of 2.5 million bags in the first six months of 1997.
Indonesian exporter officials have said they are open to talks on the African proposal but have expressed concern about losing market share to rival Vietnam, which is not an ACPC member.
Yesterday the Ivorian minister for commodities Guy-Alain Gauze said that Vietnamese officials had told him on a recent visit that the country would consider joining the ACPC.
But this morning officials in Hanoi said that while the country was considering ACPC membership, it was unlikely to do so in the near future.

Overseas traders attending the coffee seminar said the market would not be disappointed if ACPC members did not reach a decision on additional cuts. Rather the only market reaction would be if in fact member countries did agree to take further action.
"That would be a real surprise," one European trader said.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
